newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH MARKKA MAY FIRM MORE IN ERM - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH MARKKA MAY FIRM MORE IN ERM - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Significant dammed-up export revenues among Finnish exporters are likely to keep pushing the markka stronger altough the currency was linked to the ERM with a weaker-than-market central rate on Saturday, analysts said.

The initial reaction may be to test weaker ground -- the markka's 3.04 per mark central parity rate was almost two percent softer than its 2.9860 close on Friday -- but a rally is just around the corner, they said.
"If it goes to 3.00, exporters will start bringing home export revenues again," said Merita Bank chief analyst Jukka Lepomaki.
Exporters may even start buying immediately on the end of uncertainty about the link, although the rate was well in line with expectations, he added.
In a Reuters poll last Thursday of 10 financial market operators, the median as well as the most frequent entry of forecasts ranging from 3.00 to 3.052 was 3.03 per mark.
OKOBANK treasury analyst Teijo Rantatupa also saw underlying interest to buy markka.

"The initial reaction that may come on Monday ... is that it weakens temporarily but I think a lot of interest to sell (foreign) currencies has piled up which -- at the latest on Monday or Tuesday will cause the markka to rise quite strongly," he said.
The markka has underperformed other European currencies in the last three to four weeks, helped by the Bank of Finland not to strengthen more ahead of the ERM link, he noted.
But the strongest end of its ERM band -- 2.61 per mark -- is still very far away, he said.
"We may go below 2.96 at the lowest in the short term," he said.
He expected the Bank of Finland to target fluctuation that would be less than half the allowed 15 percent.
"I suspect that in practice it will be around four to six percent," he said.
A five percent band both ways would keep DEM/FIM between 2.89 and 3.19.

Trading in Singapore starting around midnight local time between Sunday and Monday will give a hint of what next week will bring -- slight weakening towards the central parity rate or gains on the back of exporters' demand.
But moves either way would not be dramatic, analysts said.

And as long as the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) project stays on track and growth lives up to expectations, there is little risk that the Bank of Finland would have to defend the markka with higher interest rates -- these may even fall in the short term, they said.
"(The 3.04 central rate) may even leave some room for interest rates to fall a little bit more," said Merita's Lepomaki.

The Bank of Finland said on Saturday the fact that all ERM countries' inflation targets are in line with the Finnish target of no more than two percent made it possible to keep monetary policy unchanged after the peg.
However, it noted that if European growth does not continue to recover and if pressures on the markka emerge, it may be forced to defend the currency by raising interest rates.
"In the short term, this is good news and in the long run it is at least not bad news," Lepomaki said.
He noted that the bank had signalled that it would react to pressures with short term interest rates rather than market intervention, which it said can only have a temporary impact.
OKOBANK's Rantatupa expected bond yields to keep converging with the German level after Finland on Wednesday brought its key tender rate in line with Buba's 3.00 percent repo.
"We have nailed ourselves to the German repo rate level, I don't know if we can go below that, maybe if the markka keeps strengthening we'll have to go below Germany," he said.

"At the long end, there will be a further narrowing of the gap over Germany so that we will get to some 40 basis points," he said. On Friday the 2006 benchmark closed 48 basis points over its German equivalent.

Now the ERM outlook is clear, actual EMU progress -- including economic performance in Finland and Europe which sets the denominator for austerity criteria ratios -- will be the most important factor driving the markka and yields.
"We will start looking at how the EMU process continues, that may be the most interesting thing to look at," Rantatupa said.
As long as EMU stays on track, the markka will not be under pressure and interest rates will track German rates although turmoil would be unevitable if EMU failed, he said.
"That would cause terrible eruptions, I don't even want to think about the whole thing," Rantatupa said.
"If all this were to be pulled apart, we're in the periphery and a neighbour to Russia: it would cause a widening yield gap, a softening markka, and higher short-term interest rates too."
